title: U.S. House · Tennessee's 8th District
area: West Tennessee, including parts of Memphis's suburbs, Jackson, and Martin, under the congressional map Tennessee redrew in May 2026.

context.text: Tennessee redrew its congressional district boundaries in May 2026 (mid-decade redistricting). Incumbent Rep. David Kustoff (R) was unopposed in the August 6, 2026 Republican primary. Heidi Kuhn won the Democratic primary with 51.8% of the vote in a four-candidate field. Seven independent candidates are also on the general-election ballot.
Ballotpedia has not published outside race ratings for this district for the 2026 cycle at the time of research; Kustoff has won this seat in five straight elections since 2016.

candidates.name: David Kustoff
candidates.ballotNote: Unopposed in the August 6 Republican primary

summary.text: David Kustoff is a Memphis-area attorney and Republican who has represented Tennessee's 8th District since January 2017. Before Congress he led Shelby County's Republican Party, served as U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Tennessee, and sat on the Tennessee Higher Education Commission. He serves on the House Committee on Ways and Means and is seeking re-election.

background.text: Born and raised in Shelby County; attended White Station High School, then earned his undergraduate degree from the University of Memphis and graduated in 1992 from its Cecil C. Humphreys School of Law.
Opened a law firm in Memphis in 1992, according to his official biography.

Served as Chairman of the Shelby County Republican Party (1995–1999) and as Tennessee chairman of Lamar Alexander's 2002 U.S. Senate campaign and of the Bush/Cheney presidential campaigns in 2000 and 2004.

Appointed U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Tennessee by President George W. Bush in 2006 and confirmed by the Senate; oversaw the majority of the Tennessee Waltz public-corruption trials that sent 12 defendants, including Sen. John Ford, to federal prison.
Joined the board of BankTennessee in 2010.

Appointed by Gov. Bill Haslam to the Tennessee Higher Education Commission in 2015, where he oversaw implementation of the Tennessee Promise last-dollar community-college scholarship program and Tennessee Reconnect.
Elected to the U.S. House in 2016 and re-elected in 2018, 2020, 2022, and 2024; he is in his fifth term and was unopposed in the August 6, 2026 Republican primary.
Serves on the House Committee on Ways and Means and its Subcommittees on Tax and Health, and chairs the House-Knesset Parliamentary Friendship Group.
Lives in Germantown with his wife, Roberta; they have two children, according to his official biography.

positions.summary: Says gun-control bills infringe on Second Amendment rights and that he will continue to oppose such efforts.
positions.quote: During my time in Congress, I have and will continue to oppose efforts that infringe on our Second Amendment rights.

positions.summary: Says abortion is wrong and he backs pro-life policies; his issues page also reports he applauded passage of a bill restricting abortion after 20 weeks.
positions.quote: I believe that life begins at conception and that abortion is wrong. As your Representative, I will continue to back pro-life policies that protect the lives of unborn children and the well-being of their mothers.

record.text: Voted against gun-control legislation in the House, saying the bills "trespass on the Second Amendment" and "place more restrictive burdens on law-abiding gun owners."
Serves on the House Committee on Ways and Means, including its Tax and Health subcommittees.

candidates.name: Heidi Kuhn
candidates.ballotNote: Won the August 6 Democratic primary with 51.8% of the vote in a four-candidate field
candidates.currentRole: Former Shelby County Criminal Court Clerk (2018–2026)

summary.text: Heidi Kuhn is a Democrat who served as Shelby County Criminal Court Clerk from 2018 until her term ended in 2026, after a career in Shelby County government that began in 2000. She lost the May 2026 Democratic primary for Shelby County mayor and won the August 6 Democratic primary for the 8th District. She describes her campaign as focused on lowering costs, supporting farmers and workers, and expanding second chances through criminal justice reform.

background.text: Earned a bachelor's degree from the University of New Mexico (a bachelor's in education, according to a news report) and a graduate degree from Christian Brothers University.
Began her career with Shelby County Government in 2000 as a health programs manager.
Elected Shelby County Criminal Court Clerk in 2018, defeating incumbent Richard DeSaussure with 58.6% of the vote; re-elected in 2022 with 62.0%.

After taking office she and colleagues found unaccounted-for checks and files, and she launched an audit of the clerk's office; she also said the office had a low number of criminal-record expungements.
Did not seek re-election as clerk in 2026; Ballotpedia lists her term as ending September 1, 2026. She ran for Shelby County mayor and lost the May 5, 2026 Democratic primary to Mickell Lowery.
Won the August 6, 2026 Democratic primary for the 8th District with 51.8% of the vote against three opponents; WSMV reports she was endorsed by outgoing Rep. Steve Cohen.
Describes herself as a lifelong public servant and community leader.

priorities.text: Says lowering the cost of living for working families is her top priority, citing groceries, housing, healthcare, and child care costs.
priorities.quote: Lowering the cost of living for working families is my top priority. Families across West Tennessee are working hard but continue to struggle with the rising costs of groceries, housing, healthcare, child care, and other everyday expenses.

priorities.text: Says supporting farmers and strengthening rural communities is a top priority, including protecting family farms and expanding rural infrastructure.
Says protecting workers' rights and supporting organized labor is a key priority.
priorities.quote: Every worker deserves fair wages, safe working conditions, and the freedom to organize and bargain collectively.

positions.summary: Campaign issues page says she would vote to raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $17 by 2030 by signing onto the Raise the Wage Act.
positions.quote: Heidi will vote to raise the minimum wage by signing onto the “Raise the Wage” act which will raise the $7.25 federal minimum wage to $17 by 2030, so that working-class Tennesseans have livable wages.

positions.summary: Campaign issues page says she would repeal cuts to Medicare and Medicaid.
positions.quote: Heidi will repeal cuts to Medicare and Medicaid that are stripping health coverage from seniors and working families across Tennessee

positions.summary: Campaign issues page says she would oppose tariffs on farm equipment and fertilizer and reject the current tariffs.
positions.quote: Heidi will oppose tariffs on equipment and fertilizer that drive up costs for Tennessee farmers and have triggered retaliatory tariffs on our exports.

candidates.name: Adam Austill

summary.text: Adam Austill is an independent candidate from Covington, Tennessee, a doctoral candidate at the University of Memphis studying American literature who works with children with autism providing ABA therapy. His campaign messages focus on limiting the influence of money in Congress, accountability, and limits on artificial intelligence.

background.text: Graduated from Covington High School.
Describes himself as a long-time Covington resident with deep family ties to West Tennessee; lives with his wife and two youngest children.
Doctoral candidate at the University of Memphis studying American literature; works providing ABA therapy for children with autism.

priorities.text: Proposes public financing of elections, ending congressional stock trading, and twelve-year term limits to limit the influence of money in Congress.
Calls for firm restrictions on artificial intelligence, including on AI-powered surveillance and data-center resource use.

candidates.researchNotes: Searched for a campaign website, questionnaire or forum coverage for Adam Austill; none found.

candidates.name: Pamela Moses

summary.text: Pamela Moses is an independent candidate who describes herself as a mother, musician, human-rights advocate, and voting-rights activist; she says a past conviction bars her from voting even though she can run for office. She received 0.8% of the vote as an independent in the 2024 U.S. Senate race in Tennessee.

background.text: Born in Kingsport, Tennessee; graduated from Central Memphis High School, earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Tennessee (2000) and a graduate degree from Union University (2007), according to Ballotpedia.
Career experience as a musician, organizer, and human-rights advocate; says she became a human-rights advocate challenging voter-disenfranchisement laws that affect people with past convictions.
Ran as an independent in the 2024 U.S. Senate election in Tennessee, receiving 24,682 votes (0.8%) in the general election won by Sen. Marsha Blackburn.

priorities.text: Campaign focuses on equal justice under the law and voting-rights restoration for people with past convictions.
Lists criminal justice reform tied to economic opportunity for formerly incarcerated people as the first of seven policy points.
priorities.quote: Pamela Moses will champion comprehensive criminal justice reform that integrates economic opportunities for justice-impacted individuals.

priorities.text: Lists expanding mental health resources, especially in underserved communities.
priorities.quote: Expanding mental health resources, particularly in underserved communities, and integrating mental health services into primary care.

positions.summary: Her campaign policy page (undated, written in the third person) says she advocates universal health care access.
positions.quote: Pamela advocates for universal healthcare access, ensuring every Tennessean receives quality medical care.

positions.summary: Her campaign policy page (undated, written in the third person) lists stricter regulation of gun manufacturing and sales.
positions.quote: Creating stricter regulations on gun manufacturing and sales, along with programs that address the social and economic factors contributing to violence.

statements.quote: Promoting green energy solutions and investments in American-made infrastructure, including a high-speed rail line that supports sustainable development, job creation, and regional connectivity.
statements.context: On her campaign website's policy page (undated; written in the third person by the campaign)

candidates.researchNotes: Positions come from the seven-point policy page on her campaign website, which is undated and is written in the third person; it may predate the 2026 redistricting. No debate or questionnaire answers found.

candidates.name: Horace Taylor

summary.text: Horace Taylor is an independent candidate and information technology professional who served in the U.S. Army from 1981 to 2012, according to his Ballotpedia profile. He says he would evaluate votes on whether they move things forward for West Tennesseans.
summary.quote: I will not be boxed in by party loyalty. I am "Independent" and independence is your greatest asset in Congress.

background.text: Graduated from Southside High School; earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Memphis (1993) and a graduate degree from the University of Maryland University College (2005), according to Ballotpedia.
Served in the U.S. Army from 1981 to 2012; works as an information technology professional.
Lists cost of living, rural healthcare access, agricultural and trade policy, rural broadband, cybersecurity, education and public safety as his policy interests.

priorities.text: Says he would break from straight party-line voting and evaluate each vote on whether it benefits West Tennesseans.

candidates.researchNotes: Searched for a campaign website, questionnaire or forum coverage for Horace Taylor; none found.
